title: Tuning the Optoelectronics of Mixed-Semiconductors through the interplay of Quantum confinement and Stoichiometry Engineering
authors: Kanha Ram Khator, Anupam Manna, Amlandeep Nayak, Pravat Nayek, Prasenjit Mal, Satyaprasad P Senanayak
abstract: All-inorganic cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) nanocrystals (NCs) have established themselves as an emerging semiconductor for next-generation optoelectronic technologies due to their unique combination of properties, such as near unity photoluminescence quantum yields, narrow color pure emission, and exceptional defect tolerance. Although size-dependent optical signatures of these NCs are well reported, the complexity of mixed ionic-electronic transport remains largely unexplored. In this study, we provide a comprehensive analysis of size-dependent charge transport by decoupling ionic and electronic transport dynamics through carefully designed transient current and space charge limited current measurements. By employing NCs of different sizes ranging from 5.6 nm to 11.3 nm in thin films, we provide a comprehensive understanding of quantum confinement effects and related synthetic chemistry. Contrary to popular beliefs of quantum confinement and band gap broadening, our results demonstrate that the smallest NCs exhibit the most efficient transport characteristics, evidenced by the lowest activation energy (hole activation energy = 78 meV) for hole transport and the highest barrier for vacancy-mediated ion migration (ion activation energy = 370 meV). This work paves a way forward for perovskite-based efficient quantum devices, by demonstrating that moving into a strong quantum confinement regime, a superior charge transport can be facilitated, when supported by carefully tailored stoichiometry.
summary: This work investigates how nanocrystal size and stoichiometry affect charge transport in $	ext{CsPbBr}_3$ perovskite semiconductors. By decoupling electronic and ionic contributions using transient measurements, the authors show that smaller NCs exhibit superior charge transport properties. This demonstrates that controlled synthesis can optimize device performance by managing both quantum confinement effects and defect-related ion migration.
main_problem: The study aims to comprehensively understand size-dependent charge transport by decoupling ionic and electronic transport dynamics in mixed-semiconductor nanocrystals.
main_result: Contrary to popular belief, the smallest $	ext{CsPbBr}_3$ NCs exhibit superior charge transport characteristics, evidenced by lower hole activation energy and higher ion migration barriers.
method: The research utilized transient current measurements and space charge limited current (SCLC) analysis on thin films of varying sizes to probe coupled electronic and ionic dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is all-inorganic cesium lead bromide ($	ext{CsPbBr}_3$) nanocrystals synthesized via controlled precursor chemistry, allowing systematic tuning of size and stoichiometry across different phases (p-, t-, d-).
key_observables: Time-of-flight mobility ($\mu_{	ext{TOF}}$), hole activation energy ($E_{a	ext{hole}}$), ion migration activation energy ($E_{a	ext{ion}}$), and characteristic time constants ($	au_c$).
important_parameters: NC size (5.6 nm to 11.3 nm), precursor chemistry, quantum confinement regime, and temperature dependence.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting transport data to Arrhenius laws for temperature dependence and using SCLC formalism for high-field electronic measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the measurement setup for transient current pulses, show temperature-dependent transient currents across different NC phases, and present $J$-$V$ characteristics used to determine activation energies for both holes and ions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates transport by first establishing the mixed-transport nature using transient measurements, then quantifying electronic mobility via SCLC, and finally characterizing ion dynamics through temperature-dependent analysis to correlate size/stoichiometry with optimal charge transport.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state optoelectronics, the detailed separation of fast electronic hopping from slower, thermally activated ionic drift provides a model for understanding coupled charge carrier dynamics in complex interfaces, relevant to open quantum systems modeling.
